name: Symbolic Computation

papers.title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
papers.abstract: This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations. We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gr\"obner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.

papers.title: Partial Homogenization and the Structure of Optimal Algebraic Algorithms
papers.abstract: A quadratic map, such as the product of two polynomials, two complex numbers or two matrices, is classically computed by products of two linear forms. By Strassen's homogenization, their least number is also the least number of product gates of fan-in two. With unbounded fan-in, terms of higher degree can cancel, so the classical lower bounds and classifications do not apply. We ask whether unbounded fan-in beats fan-in two, and what the optimal circuits are. Our tool is constant-free partial homogenization, which keeps the terms of higher degree. Let a quadratic map have $K$ independent outputs. We prove that, under a mild condition, unbounded fan-in needs as many product gates as fan-in two whenever fan-in two needs at most $K+2$. For $2\times2$ matrix multiplication, we classify all optimal circuits with fan-in two and arbitrary constants. We prove that none of them nests products, and that their quadratic parts are Strassen's algorithm, one new algorithm, the Waksman-type algorithms, or a one-parameter family. Over $\mathbb{R}$, we prove that unbounded fan-in needs at least $6$ product gates, and approximate circuits exactly $5$. Below the threshold $K+2$, we prove that optimal circuits are rigid, for every fan-in. Every optimal circuit for polynomial multiplication is Toom-Cook at unisolvent points, up to constant scalings and shifts. Every optimal circuit for a tubal ring over $\mathbb{C}$ applies its transform. Every optimal circuit for complex multiplication over $\mathbb{R}$ is Gauss's algorithm at three real points, after a rotation. In at least two variables, every optimal division-free homogeneous component extractor is Ben-Or's construction with shifted points. Above the threshold, for $c\ge2$ complex products over $\mathbb{R}$, we prove that fan-in two needs exactly $3c$ product gates, unbounded fan-in at least $2c+2$, and approximate circuits exactly $2c+1$.
